title: Bebop's lack of public audience and Louis Jordan
summary: No clubs for bebop, people could not dance to it; Louis Jordan's small band broke up big bands.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yeah. I mean, you could buy a house now at eighteen. So you were going to lose the house, you were going to, and you're behind your pay- Oh yeah, I'm behind my pay- All because this music called bebop, you were going to take off and you were just going to play that music. Well how popular was that music in the city? I mean, at the time.

It wasn't. Just among musicians, all the musicians. Like if you didn't play bebop, you were in the square. The guys your age wouldn't be bothered with you. So it was just sort of in the musicians themselves,
but it really hadn't, but the general public. Now I always think that man, we can educate

the public to jazz. I said, yeah, I mean to bebop. We can educate them to bebop. Then I started thinking when I got older, I said that was some funny thinking. You know, like when you got a job doing something, you're not going there to teach, to educate the people to jazz. You're going there to make some money to play something that the people like to hear. So I called up all these old musicians and told them I was ready to play again. And I started playing. What did they say? Oh you're not playing any more bebop? I told you about that dog on bebop. But man, I used to tell people, they say, well, I said, if Disney, because that's been Charlie Parker, they didn't have a penny to spend for food. They could come to my house and eat. And one time I didn't even have food to eat. My wife and I would sit down there, man, and be hungry. A guy called me up for a job. I said, man, I don't want to play and I'm hungry. I don't want to play. I don't want to play that old time music. You guys playing. So you considered that all antiquated, dictated? Yeah. But now I think about bebop now. Bebop is older to this music they play now than that kind of music they were playing then, because that was about ten years apart. But now like bebop, that's over fifty years ago. Right. Late forties. That man, like hand clapping, if you forgot, playing music, or sitting out listening to the music, clapping then, man look at that square. You had to be cool, you know. You had to be cool.
But were there any clubs that you tried to do this bebop that you could get a gig? No. There weren't any. Okay. So there weren't any.

The people didn't like the music, because they couldn't dance to it. But see, now that's the thing that really broke up the big bands. See, they had big bands to come and play. Now I said Dizzy Gillespie and Louis Jordan broke up the big bands. Dizzy Gillespie had a big band and the people couldn't dance to his music. So Louis Jordan came out with five pieces, and they would play music that people liked to hear and they would like to dance to. So the people would hire Louis Jordan, because he named but five pieces. And he would pack, any place he played, it was a packout, it was a sellout. And people said, well I can get Louis Jordan, I don't have to get Count Bates. And Lionel Hampton for this job. They got sixteen, seventeen pieces. This guy just got five pieces. And he said, we don't want Dizzy Gillespie because nobody can dance to his music.
